Guided Inquiry

1. Set the stage

A parallel-plate capacitor sits with vacuum between its plates. The battery has pushed Q₀ onto the top plate and −Q₀ onto the bottom, holding a potential difference of V₀ = 12 V across the gap.

Its capacitance is C₀ = Q₀/V₀ = 88.5 pF — the charge it stores per volt across it. A dielectric is an insulator whose molecules polarise in a field; sliding one into the gap always raises C.

2. Disconnect the battery — then predict

The battery is now disconnected — the wires are cut. With the slab fully out, Q sits at Q₀ = 1.06 nC and V reads 12 V.

You now slide the slab (κ = 4) all the way in. What happens to the voltmeter reading V?

3. Now watch it

The battery is disconnected. Slide the slab in and read the voltmeter as it moves. With κ = 4 it should collapse from 12 V to 3 V, exactly V₀/κ.

Q on the plates has not budged — the wires are cut. What rose was C; V had to fall to compensate.

4. Reconnect the battery

The battery is reconnected. It now pins V at 12 V no matter what — so as C rises with the slab, the battery pumps more charge onto the plates.

Slide the slab in and watch: V holds, Q grows. With κ = 4 the charge goes from 1.06 nC to 4.25 nC.

5. The one thing to notice

Try both switch positions side by side. At any slab position:

• Battery connected: V is pinned; Q grows.
• Battery disconnected: Q is frozen; V collapses.

What rises in both cases is C. Which of Q and V follows it and which stays put is decided entirely by whether the battery is still there.

01

At a glance

A slab of insulator slides into the gap of a charged parallel-plate capacitor, and you choose whether the battery stays connected. The sim reads out the capacitance, the charge and the voltage while the slab moves.

What you'll learn

  • How the capacitance depends on how far the slab is in and on its dielectric constant κ.
  • How the battery switch decides what the charge Q and the voltage V do as the slab moves.
  • Where the induced charges on the slab's faces come from, and what they do to the field.
A slab of dielectric constant κ enters the gap from the left. x is how far in it is, and L is the plate length.

What's on screen

  • Top plate (orange) carries +Q, and the bottom plate (blue) carries −Q.
  • Dielectric slab (violet), labelled κ, with induced rows of charge on its two faces.
  • Field arrows between the plates, labelled length ∝ E.
  • Battery and voltmeter on the wires, plus a Readouts panel for C, Q and V.
See itSlide the κ = 4 slab halfway in. Watch for: the slab covering the left half of the gap, and C reading 221.4 pF.

03

Capacitance rises steadily as the slab slides in

The part of the plates over the slab and the part over empty gap behave as two capacitors side by side, so their capacitances add. The slab part has capacitance κε₀A(x/L)/d, and the empty part has ε₀A(1 − x/L)/d. Together:

C = C₀ [1 + (κ − 1) x / L]
C₀ = ε₀A/d is the capacitance with no slab.

At x = 0 this gives C₀, and at x = L it gives κC₀. In between C is a straight line in x. With κ = 4:

x / L00.250.50.751
C / C₀11.752.53.254
C88.5 pF154.9 pF221.4 pF287.8 pF354.2 pF

Each quarter of insertion adds the same 0.75 C₀ here, which is (κ − 1)/4.

See itSlide the κ = 4 slab all the way in. Watch for: C climbing in equal steps up to 354.2 pF, which is 4.00 × C₀.
04

With the battery disconnected, V falls as the slab enters

Once the wires are cut, the plates are isolated. The charge on them stays at the value it had when you pressed Disconnected, and the voltmeter reads V = Q/C. Starting from no slab, Q = Q₀ and

V = Q₀ / C = V₀ / [1 + (κ − 1) x / L]
Q stays fixed, C rises, so V falls.
  • Slab halfway in, κ = 4: V = 12 / 2.5 = 4.8 V.
  • Slab fully in: V = V₀/κ, which is 3 V for κ = 4 and 1.5 V for κ = 8.
  • The charge is whatever it was at the cut. Disconnect with the slab already in and Q is that larger value. Changing κ afterwards changes V but never Q.
See itDisconnect with no slab, then push the κ = 4 slab in. Watch for: V falling from 12 V to 3.00 V while Q stays at 1.06 nC.
05

With the battery connected, Q grows as the slab enters

A connected battery holds the voltage across the plates at V₀ = 12 V whatever the capacitance does. So the charge has to follow C:

Q = C V₀ = Q₀ [1 + (κ − 1) x / L]
V stays fixed, C rises, so Q rises.
  • Slab halfway in, κ = 4: Q = 2.5 × 1.06 = 2.66 nC.
  • Slab fully in: Q = κQ₀, which is 4.25 nC for κ = 4. The battery has pushed 3.19 nC of extra charge onto the plates.
  • The field between the plates is V₀/d the whole time, so the field arrows keep their length.
See itConnect the battery and push the κ = 4 slab in. Watch for: Q climbing from 1.06 nC to 4.25 nC while V stays at 12.00 V.
06

Induced surface charge weakens the field in the slab

The field of the plates polarises the slab's molecules. That leaves a layer of negative charge on the face next to the positive plate and positive charge on the other face. These induced layers are the rows labelled induced in the sim.

The induced layer cancels part of the free charge, so the net sheet charge σf − σb is smaller.

For a slab of constant κ the induced charge is σb = σf (κ − 1)/κ, so the net is σf/κ and the field inside the slab is E = σf/(κε₀). For κ = 4, three quarters of the plate charge is cancelled. Under the slab the plates hold κ times as much free charge per area as under the gap, yet E = V/d is the same in both regions.

See itPut the slab fully in and lower κ from 8 to 1. Watch for: the induced rows on the slab thinning out until they disappear at κ = 1.0.
07

Where it matters

  • Capacitors for circuits. A dielectric between the plates lets a small capacitor hold much more charge for the same voltage. Ceramic, paper and electrolytic capacitors all rely on this.
  • Level gauges. A fuel or water level between two plates acts like the slab here. The liquid raises C in proportion to its height, so measuring C gives the level.
  • Touch and humidity sensors. A finger or damp air changes the dielectric near a pair of electrodes, and the circuit senses the change in C.
Go deeper: the slab is pulled in

With the battery disconnected, the stored energy Q²/(2C) falls as C rises, by a factor κ when the slab is fully in. The fringing field at the plate edge pulls the slab in, and the energy lost is the work it does. The sim does not display energy.

08

Summary

In one line. A slab changes a capacitor's C by the factor 1 + (κ − 1)x/L, and the battery switch decides how Q and V share that change.

Key points

  • C = C₀[1 + (κ − 1)x/L], from C₀ with no slab to κC₀ with the slab fully in.
  • Battery connected: V = V₀ is fixed and Q = CV₀.
  • Battery disconnected: Q is fixed at its value when the wires were cut, and V = Q/C.
  • Fully in from no slab: Q is multiplied by κ with the battery on, and V is divided by κ with it off.

Common mix-ups

  • "A dielectric always adds charge to the plates." Only a connected battery can supply it. Once the wires are cut, Q cannot change.
  • "A dielectric always boosts the field, so V rises." The induced charges oppose the plate charge, so for the same free charge the field in the slab is smaller.
  • "Disconnecting the battery changes C." C depends only on the geometry and κ. The switch changes Q and V, not C.

Things to try on your own

  • Disconnect with the slab halfway in at κ = 4, then slide it fully in, and compare the final V with the 3 V from no slab.
  • Disconnect with no slab, push the slab fully in, then step κ through 1, 2, 4 and 8 and check V = 12/κ each time.
  • Find a κ and an x/L that give C = 2 C₀, then check the Q reading with the battery connected.
